svg.title: Loaded when it applies, not before
svg.desc: Three levels. Each bar is everything that exists at that level; the highlighted part is what actually gets loaded. Nearly all of the first level loads, a small share of the second, and a sliver of the third. Drawn as three levels for clarity, though the real hierarchy is ragged and of arbitrary depth.

g.font-family: ui-sans-serif, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
g.text: Loaded when it applies, not before
Each bar is everything at that level. Only the highlighted part is loaded. Three levels for clarity — the real hierarchy is ragged.
nearly all of it, every run
The conventions that apply whatever you are doing. Small on purpose —
if this grows without limit, the whole idea stops working.
the one that matched
the rest of your guidance, not loaded
The instructions for the job in hand, picked by matching the task.
You may have hundreds. One or two get loaded.
reference material — opened by name, a page at a time
Schema details, source documents, past decisions. Far more of this
exists than of the two above, and far less of it is ever read.
Why bother
A context window is
attention, not storage.
Filling it with material
that does not apply
makes answers worse,
not just pricier.
So what gets picked
is the hard part.
Bars are drawn the same width so the shrinking share is visible. The real amounts grow sharply going down.
